summary: Every year NASA retires hardware that was never designed to come home — satellites left in orbit, landers left on the Moon, gloves lost in spacewalks. We built Abandoned in Place, a "night museum" that walks visitors through this hidden heritage. The site is a single-page interactive experience: a 3D Mars landscape greets you with EVA-1, an animated astronaut curator who tours you through the halls. Twenty curated exhibits tell true stories of discarded equipment (Vanguard 1, Ed White's lost glove, Launch Complex 34, Skylab, the Golden Records), each with a full dossier: why it was abandoned, where it is now, and what legacy it left. Around the galleries sit six decades of interactive timeline history, a narrated Story Vault audio theatre, a live orbit map, a real-time debris "Reality Check", a museum quiz that issues a personalized certificate, a visitor Relic Wall, and The Graveyard Shift — a five-mission recovery game where you rescue dying satellites. The Live Archive searches NASA's own image library in real time, so every claim is checkable.
details:
What it does / how it works. Abandoned in Place reimagines space heritage as an explorable museum. On arrival, EVA-1 — an animated 3D astronaut guide — greets you and offers a guided tour through every hall. The galleries contain 20 researched exhibits of real discarded NASA hardware. The Mission Reels are three chaptered 3D films (Moon, Mars, Deep Space); the Story Vault is a radio-drama audio theatre with narrated story reels; the Timeline charts six decades of spaceflight; the Orbit Map and Reality Check visualize live orbital positions and the debris problem; the quiz grades you and issues a personalized certificate; the Relic Wall lets visitors leave messages for future archaeologists; and The Graveyard Shift turns orbital clean-up into a five-mission recovery game with real mission briefs drawn from history. The Live Archive performs live searches against NASA's Image and Video Library API, connecting every story to primary-source imagery.

Benefits and intended impact. The project turns "space junk" from an afterthought into a story about human ambition — making space heritage, orbital debris, and mission archaeology emotionally engaging and verifiable. Visitors leave understanding that everything we launch stays somewhere, and that preserving, tracking, and cleaning up that history matters.

Tools and technologies. Next.js 16 (App Router) with TypeScript, React Three Fiber / three.js for 3D scenes, Tailwind CSS 4 with shadcn/ui, Framer Motion for animation, Prisma with SQLite for exhibits/quiz/notes data, Bun as the runtime, and FFmpeg for video production. AI tools were used for code development, AI-generated poster illustrations, and AI text-to-speech narration.

Creativity and considered factors. The museum conceit (catalog numbers, curator notes, plaques, a gift-shop tone) is the creative spine; EVA-1 guides different visitors differently. We considered accessibility (semantic HTML, ARIA, keyboard navigation, reduced-motion support), fact accuracy (stories checked against NASA sources), responsible AI use (stories drafted with AI then hand-checked; AI art used only where no NASA photo exists; no NASA insignia or branding in any generated asset), and performance (lazy 3D loading, cached narration audio).
